ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
3 
 
1. Overview 
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the 
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within 
the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). 
 
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. James G. Quintiere of the Department of Fire 
Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland.  The experiment has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is), 
namely Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, of the same U. Maryland department, and Dr. John L. de Ris (FM Global, 
retired).  The ISS research also benefitted greatly from the work of Parham Dehghani, a doctoral student 
in the Fire Protection Engineering department. 
 
Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME 
including BRE and the rest of the ACME investigations.  In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki 
Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist.  For 
ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam 
who are also with CWRU. 
 
The ISS operations were conducted in two separate rounds of testing during Increments 58-59 and 63-64.  
More specifically, the first round of testing was conducted from Feb. to April 2019, while the second-
round testing occurred from Sept. 2020 to Jan. 2021.  The first round of tests was limited to ethylene and 
the 25-mm BRE burner, while the second round also included tests with methane and the 50-mm burner 
(although not together). 
 
 
2. Science Overview 
A. Background 
This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document 
(SRD) of June 2013. 
 
The goal of this research is to establish the burning conditions possible in a microgravity quiescent 
environment.  The approach is to do this using a burner to emulate (BRE, Burning Rate Emulator) 
the burning for real condensed fuels, representative of common liquids and solids.  This will be 
done for quasi-steady burning conditions, albeit ideal in some cases, but the BRE will range over 
a wide spectrum of real fuel properties.  The key properties governing steady burning are (1) the 
heat of gasification, (2) the surface re-radiation heat flux, and (3) the heat of combustion.  Flame 
radiation is also relevant in general and can be represented in terms of the laminar smoke point. 
Its importance in microgravity flames needs study, but the first three properties are key. 
 
Currently NASA assesses the flammability hazard of materials for use in space flight by an upward 
flame spread “pass-fail” test (Test 1), and supplements with data from the Cone Calorimeter (Test 
2).  The latter test has the capability of measuring the three properties listed above.  Hence, the 
successful application of the BRE in microgravity can enhance the usefulness of Test 2. 
 
Fundamental and ad hoc testing in microgravity at quiescent conditions has shown that quasi-
steady flames can be supported on candle-wicks, droplets, jets and, at very low ambient velocities, 
small plastic samples and a burner flame.  The established flames tend to have spherical or semi-

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
4 
 
ellipsoidal shapes. Our preliminary work burning ethanol on planar wicks of 1 × 4 cm suggest 
similar shapes in aircraft and drop tower tests.  But this work showed instabilities in the drop 
tower, and needs further exploration.  Theoretical analysis based on microgravity jet flame length 
correlations suggests that a 50 mm diameter planar material could support quasi-steady 
combustion in microgravity for some liquid and plastic fuels.  The analysis indicates that burning 
depends on diameter, so several additional burner sizes will be needed to examine this effect. 
 
Gas burners like the BRE have been used to successfully simulate burning of a wide range of fuels 
in terms of their B numbers and configurations over a range of Grashof numbers.  We have 
successfully shown that for planar burning at different angle orientations that a burner can 
emulate the flame standoff distribution, and even match the onset of unsteadiness to turbulent 
flow.  Theoretical analyses of such a problem are limited by the inability to accurately deal with 
flame radiation, turbulence and variable properties.  A burner simulation can be far superior as it 
inherently contains these effects. 
 
The construction of a 50 mm diameter prototype BRE burner with flame heat flux sensors has 
enabled us to emulate both a methanol and heptane pool fire of the 50 mm diameter, reproducing 
its color, flame character and shape, and heat of gasification for nearly the same surface 
temperatures.  We show that the BRE is capable of displaying the burning conditions in terms of 
the fuel properties of heat of combustion, heat of gasification, and surface re-radiant heat flux 
(with some likely effect of smoke point).  A preliminary 3-D plot of steady burning gives a 
flammability mapping in terms of these variables under conditions of gravity and atmospheric 
variations.  A mapping in microgravity can demonstrate the burning conditions for a wide range 
of real materials in terms of these properties.  In addition the effect of external radiation can 
indirectly be assessed.  The 50 mm burner has been redesigned, along with a 25 mm burner, to 
reduce edge effects, provide improved heat flux sensors with temperatures, and cooling water 
has been dropped from the both the burner and the heat flux sensors in microgravity 
experiments. 
 
The primary objective is to observe the burning behavior (including extinction) in long-duration 
microgravity for methane/nitrogen and ethylene/nitrogen mixtures on a porous circular burner 
of 25 and 50 mm diameter at various pressures, ambient oxygen, and CO2 (desired, to assess 
extinguishment).  Ignition will not be directly studied in microgravity studies, as we believe 
normal-gravity experiments are sufficient for its study.  Another objective is to obtain conditions 
that can be related to microgravity behavior of condensed fuels that embrace the scope of real 
liquid and solid fuels. 
 
We think these results can establish fuel properties that directly relate to the fire hazard in 
spacecraft, and these properties can be derived from NASA Test 2.  The BRE is an efficient, safe, 
and comprehensive technique for achieving these results. 
 
This version of the Science Requirements Document has been refined since the Science Concept 
Review (Aug 28, 2012).  The panel wrote at that time that they “strongly encourage continued 
development of the BRE experiment for implementation into the ACME and testing on the ISS.” 
We have tried to address most of their recommendations and suggestions.  In addition, work has 
progressed to include the development of two papers, and the commencement of drop facility 
testing of the BRE.  Those results have shown quasi-steady flames, and are very encouraging.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
5 
 
B. Rationale for Microgravity 
This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity’ section (2.5) of the experiment’s SRD 
from June 2013.  Equations are not included here, but they can be found in the SRD. 
 
Fire in a spacecraft microgravity environment is a likely event based on limited accident data, tests 
to burn materials, and research that has explored simple burning scenarios.  Indeed, NASA screens 
the use of materials on spacecraft by its flammability Test 1. 
 
Currently NASA Test 1 and Test 2 are incapable of directly analyzing material fire hazards in 
spacecraft. There is no predictive methodology to extrapolate from these tests.  However, NASA 
Test 2, the Cone Calorimeter, is capable of determining heats of combustion and gasification, and 
surface reradiation in burning. Steady (or quasi-steady) burning rate data from the BRE in flight 
experiments will establish a flammability mapping in terms of these properties for microgravity. 
In addition, using Eq. (2), the results can establish the necessary heat flux condition for other fuels 
to burn in microgravity.  The BRE is an efficient way to achieve quasi-steady burning. While 
microgravity tests of condensed fuels have been performed and are planned, they are limited in 
their ability to reveal sufficient information about the diverse condensed fuels that exist aboard 
the ISS.  Moreover the time to achieve quasi-steady burning rate of solid fuels can be of the order 
of minutes as dictated by the time response of the solid.  The BRE can be turned on and off quickly, 
and its quasi-steady condition is only dependent on the gas phase phenomenon.  While this time 
is shorter, it can still be on the order of 10 seconds or more. 
 
The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft owing to considerable g-jitter 
disturbances.  While limited testing is possible in drop facilities, the characteristic times for the 
gas phase (approximately 20 s) and the burner surface temperature (approximately 40 s) preclude 
consideration of quasi-steady conditions.  Preliminary testing in the NASA 5.2 s drop facility 
indicated the approach to quasi-steady burning, but longer tests are needed to confirm this 
tendency.  The longer duration testing in the ISS with the efficient operation of the BRE can 
produce results only limited by the gas-phase response time. 
 
C. Science Objectives 
The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section (2.2) of the 
experiment’s SRD from June 2013.  ISS testing was not carried out to address the desired second 
objective, where NASA effectively limited this experiment to the first and third objectives. 
 
The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity 
ambient in terms of material properties.  The specific flight objectives are as follows. 
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter.  Consider O2/N2 
ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures.  NASA-
considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % 
oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.  Emphasize fuel conditions that can 
be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. 
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.

6 
 
D. Science Success Criteria 
This text is from the BRE portion of the ‘Success Criteria’ section of the ACME Integrated Science 
Requirements Document (ISRD, ACME-SRD-001.B) from Sept. 2013, which is revision B of the 
version prepared for the Requirements Definition Review (RDR).  Achievement of superior success, 
as defined below, was effectively ruled out by NASA because its plan didn’t include the desired 
tests. 
 
6.5.1.  Minimum Success 
- Obtain color video, burner surface temperature, and burner heat flux for two C2H4 
flames that burn for at least 20 s and then extinguish. 
6.5.2.  High Success 
All of the above plus: 
- Obtain a flammability map for C2H4. 
6.5.3.  Complete Success 
All of the above plus: 
- Obtain a flammability map for CH4. 
- Measure peak temperatures (using filament and/or soot pyrometry) as a function of 
time for at least 5 flames. 
- Measure temperature distributions (using filament and/or soot pyrometry) at or near 
quasi-steady conditions for at least 5 flames. 
- Measure temperature distributions (using filament pyrometry) near the extinction 
limit for at least 5 flames. 
- Measure soot volume fraction profiles at (or near) quasi-steady conditions and near 
the extinction limit for at least 5 flames. 
6.5.4.  Superior Success 
All of the above plus: 
- Complete the desired parts of the test matrix.

3. Hardware Overview 
A. General Description 
This section is copied from section 2.A of the April 2021 version of ‘ACME Engineering 
Implementation’ which should be consulted for additional details.  References to other sections 
within the boxed text of this section refer to the ACME Engineering Implementation document. 
 
This section provides a general description a general description of the ACME engineering from 
the ‘3.0 Experimental’ section of the following 2014 conference paper: 
Dennis P. Stocker, Fumiaki Takahashi, J. Mark Hickman, and Andrew C. Suttles, “Gaseous 
Non-Premixed Flame Research Planned for the International Space Station,” Spring 
Technical Meeting of the Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Tulsa, OK, 16–
18 March 2014. 
 
IMPORTANT: The 2104 paper from which this section was extracted proceeded completion of the 
spaceflight hardware which was mostly launched in 2017.  As a result, it does not accurately 
describe the final engineering in some regards.   Therefore updates, clarifications, additional 
details, shortcomings, references, etc. have been included in boxed notes like this following the 
original description.  As a minor note, the sizes of figures were adjusted in this report, but none 
were cropped. 
 
As previously discussed, the ACME experiments will be conducted within the Combustion 
Integrated Rack (CIR) using a chamber insert, depicted in Figure 2, which was designed to 
accommodate gas delivery to a variety of exchangeable burners.  Besides the chamber insert, 
other ACME-unique hardware includes a high-definition color camera and an avionics package, 
which is for data acquisition and control. 
 
 
Figure 2: Design of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) chamber 
insert that will be used in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on ISS.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
8 
 
ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of 
burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter.  As 
depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 
to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 
and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two 
flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm).  Most burners 
will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux 
transducers.  The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring 
of the pressure differential across the outlet surface.  The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable 
tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for 
precise positioning. 
 
 
Figure 3: ACME burner types, including from left to right, gas-jet burners, a co-flow burner, 
porous spherical burners, and flat porous burners for the BRE experiment. 
 
Ultimately, the spherical burners were limited to a single diameter of 6.35 mm, and the fabricated 
gas-jet burners were limited to two sizes with nominal inner diameters of 1.3 and 2.1 mm.  
However, only the larger gas-jet burner was used during the spaceflight tests.  The burners are 
addressed in detail in section 3.C. 
 
Unfortunately, the spherical burners have not always yielded spherically symmetric flames, 
presumably as a result of (1) greater burner flow through the joint between the porous sphere and 
supply tube, and (2) heat loss to the support tube (encompassing the supply tube) causing local 
flame quenching. 
 
Two types of igniter tips have been used during ACME testing.  Most tests have been conducted 
using a loop igniter tip like those which had been successfully used in the droplet combustion 
experiments which preceded ACME research in the CIR.  However, some tests were conducted with 
a coil igniter tip, where that included the second round testing for both the Burning Rate Emulator 
(BRE) and Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiments, with the 
exception of the latter’s first day testing.  The CFI-G investigation will also use the coil igniter tip.  
For more information about the igniter tips, see section 3.D. 
 
The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the 
delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner.  The 
maximum fuel flow is 2 slpm (on a nitrogen basis), whereas much higher flows, e.g., 10 slpm (on 
a nitrogen basis), are possible for the oxidizer and nitrogen lines.  The crew can exchange the mass 
flow controllers to provide appropriate ranges that maximize the flow accuracy.  The gas delivery 
system enables on-orbit dilution of the fuel or oxidizer (but not both simultaneously), coflow, 
inverse flames (e.g., oxidizer delivery to the center of a coflow burner), and premixed flames,

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
9 
 
although the latter are not planned for any of the current ACME experiments.  Gases can also be 
delivered premixed to the space station where that is necessary in some circumstances, such as 
the blending of different fuel gases.  CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME 
will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) 
that can be released into the combustion chamber. 
 
Thus far, ACME tests were not conducted with carbon dioxide as a diluent.  Furthermore, the fuel 
diluted with helium was premixed prior to launch rather than on orbit.  Ultimately, oxidizer flows 
of up to 20 slpm (on a nitrogen basis) were possible, while the nitrogen flow was limited to a 
maximum of 5 slpm.  ACME has not used gas bottles smaller than 1 liter as indicated above; the 
bottle fill pressure was instead limited as an additional hazard control.  
 
ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and 
two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in 
use on orbit.  All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber.  Collectively, the 
imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot 
volume fraction; and operational support.  However, it is unlikely that all functions would be 
exercised at any one time as will become apparent in the subsequent discussion. 
 
Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of 
the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning 
mirror).  Both cameras are part of the ACME hardware that is now in development.  The analog 
camera signal will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations.  Light-
emitting diodes within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both 
support the operations and provide reference images.  The 12-bit digital camera records at up to 
30 full frames (1360x1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent 
control of the zoom, iris, and focus.  The digital camera will be equipped with a filter assembly 
with four options, where selection of a clear “filter” allows for color imaging.  Color imaging can 
also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to 
avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green.  The natural flame 
color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is pyrometry and 
measurement of the soot volume fraction, again via the techniques of [23-24].  Alternately, CH* 
imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm 
bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM).  A 450-nm 
bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract 
interfering broadband soot emission.  However, the filter assembly rotates slowly so such 
subtraction effectively requires a separate test with each filter and of course reproducible flame 
conditions. 
 
The video from the analog operations (i.e., ops) camera, also referred to as the internal camera, 
is not archived in space.  The video is instead recorded on the ground in the operations center.  Its 
gain was sometimes adjusted for improved imaging of dim flames, e.g., approaching extinction.   
 
The sensitivity of the color digital camera, often referenced as the ACME DataCam (i.e., Data 
Camera), to the dim microgravity flames was such that it was often used with long exposure times 
and thus low framing rates, for example on the order of 1 frame per second.  The clear “filter” is 
of fused silica.  Unfortunately, the thickness of the blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter and the added

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
10 
 
antireflective (AR) coating caused too great a reduction in the red, so it does not balance the 
intensity of the three color planes as intended and thereby can limit the accuracy of temperature 
determination.  Meanwhile, rather than the 450-nm bandpass filter described above, the high 
definition color camera was equipped with a bandpass filter for imaging formaldehyde emissions.   
For more information, see the Data Camera Characterization Report (ACME-RPT-010 Rev. A).   
 
Imaging of the dim hydrogen flames in the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames 
(s-Flame) experiment was particularly challenging with these, if not all, cameras.   
 
Pyrometry can alternately be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral 
(HiBMs) camera, equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF), which allows for imaging at 
multiple spectra, but requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired band.  This 
camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512x512 and 30 frames per second 
(fps).  Although it has a 1024x1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss 
through the LCTF.  Both soot pyrometry and Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) are possible, where 
ACME is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers.  The fibers are 
orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired 
position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video.  During set 
up, the crew can manually orient the array so that it is orthogonal to either ACME’s color digital 
camera or the HiBMs camera with the LCTF.  An alternate fiber array including a platinum wire 
will be used for inflight characterization, which in combination with preflight calibration will 
enable determination of the soot volume fraction [24]. 
 
In contrast to the preceding paragraph, ACME did not use a HiBMs camera for pyrometry, but 
instead relied on use of ACME’s color DataCam for such temperature measurements.  For an 
example of how this can be done, see the techniques described in the following papers:   
P.B. Kuhn, B. Ma, B.C. Connelly, M.D. Smooke, and M.B. Long, “Soot and Thin-filament Pyrometry 
Using a Color Digital Camera,” Proceedings of the Combustion Institute, 33 (2011) 743-750.  
B. Ma, M. B. Long, “Absolute light calibration using S-type thermocouples,” Proceedings of the 
Combustion Institute, 34 (2) (2013) 3531-3539. 
 
Thus far, TFP tests have been conducted with 14-micron fibers spaced apart by 5 mm for a total 
span of 20 mm (in the case of 5 intact ceramic fibers), neglecting optional translation of the array.  
Tests have been conducted using arrays with and without the platinum wire in the furthest 
downstream position.  Tests have also been conducted with some of the fibers broken and 
subsequently removed, leaving only three fibers in the final testing for the BRE and Coflow Laminar 
Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiments and at least the initial testing for the Cool Flames 
Investigation with Gases (CFI-G). 
 
CIR has a second HiBMs camera, without a filter, that will be used in combination with CIR’s 
illumination package for alternate measurements of the soot volume fraction.  This will be 
accomplished via an extinction technique previously employed in microgravity [3,6,26], where the 
camera and the collimated light source (with its two fiber-coupled laser diodes) are positioned at 
opposite windows.  The images are recorded at 1024x1024 and 30 fps.  Thus far, the primary 
purpose of this combined system has been the measurement of the droplet diameter for 
determination of the droplet burning rate.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
11 
 
A HiBMs camera without the Liquid Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) has been used throughout much, 
but not all, of ACME’s operations.  In the first round of the CLD Flame experiment, it was used 
without a filter for flame imaging, but this proved to be largely unsuccessful because the camera 
is very insensitive to blue.  Afterward, it was equipped with a red filter corresponding to the CIR 
illumination package for the rest of the ACME testing.  Unfortunately, that filter is sufficiently 
broad that significant incandescence can pass through the filter limiting its utility for 
determinations of soot volume fraction via light extinction, e.g., through the technique described 
in the following papers: 
D.L. Urban, Z.G. Yuan, P.B. Sunderland, K.C., Lin, Z. Dai, and G.M. Faeth, “Smoke-Point Properties 
of Nonbuoyant Round Laminar Jet Diffusion Flames,” Proceedings of the Twenty-Eighth 
Symposium (International) on Combustion 28 (2000) 1965-1972.  
F.J. Diez, C. Aalburg, P.B. Sunderland, D.L. Urban, Z.-G. Yuan, G.M. Faeth, “Soot properties of 
laminar jet diffusion flames in microgravity,” Combustion and Flame, 156 (2009) 1514-1524.  
P.S. Greenberg and J.C. Ku, “Soot Volume Fraction Imaging,” Applied Optics, 36 (22) (1997) 5514-
5522. 
Nonetheless, soot volume fraction can also be determined from the color DataCam images. 
 
During ACME operations, the HiBMs camera is typically archived at 15 fps because of data limits 
for transfer and downlink operations.  And because operations are constrained by the data limits, 
image data from this camera are sometimes deleted without downlinking to enable additional 
testing.  And in some testing, HiBMs images aren’t even acquired given their lesser value. 
 
Unfortunately, the HiBMs backlight illumination is significantly obstructed by the bracket for the 
electrode mesh further limiting its utility for the E-FIELD Flames experiment.   This was a design 
trade-off necessitated primarily by ACME’s large number of cameras and other optical 
instruments. 
 
CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package is a monochrome camera with an intensifier 
(for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging.  Again as 
a result of the signal loss through the filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are 
recorded at 512x512 and 30 fps. 
 
During ACME operations, the LLL-UV camera has only been used for the Structure and Response 
of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment. 
 
While not discussed in the preceding section, another intensified camera was used throughout 
ACME testing, although its image data was sometimes deleted or not even acquired to allow the 
performance of additional tests.   This was the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) camera which was 
generally configured with its CH* filter, where an exception is some s-Flame testing with 
particularly dim flames.  Due to design trade-offs, its Field of View (FOV) was partially obstructed 
by the arms of the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array when it was moved inwards to the 
flame.  More information about this camera can be found in its characterization report, CIR-RPT-
4600. 
 
The ACME chamber insert will also be equipped with non-imaging optical diagnostics including 
both thermopile radiometers and Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs).  There is a crew-exchangeable 
linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of

1 Feb. 2022 
12 
 
experiments.  The array has a fixed position which is parallel to the chamber axis and centered 
(along the chamber length) relative to the chamber windows and thus most of the other 
instrumentation.  One array is equipped with a single wide-view radiometer with two narrow-
view radiometers that are downstream and two more that are upstream, where all views are 
orthogonal to the chamber axis, as depicted in Figure 4.  The narrow-view radiometers are 
intended to support studies of gas-jet flames, where ACME can accommodate shorter burners, 
making the “lower” detectors useful.  The other array, also seen in Fig. 4, provides for three wide-
view measurements of the flame, where one view is masked to nominally block radiant emission 
from the burner.  It was specifically designed for the BRE experiment but will be a resource 
available to other ACME experiments.  Given that the radiometer array can be exchanged by the 
crew, alternate arrays could be developed.   
 
 
Figure 4: Crew-exchangeable radiometer arrays on the ACME chamber insert: (top) standard 
(ACME) array of 5 radiometers, and (bottom) array with three radiometers, designed for the BRE 
experiment, where the lowest detector is masked to avoid view of the burner.

B. Hardware Shortcomings 
In terms of hardware, BRE’s primary challenge was that the sensors for measuring the thermal 
radiation, which had fixed amplification, often saturated.  Although the measurements were not 
documented as required to meet experiment success, they were considered sufficiently critical 
that BRE was equipped with its own radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.  
Estimates had been made of the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases 
tend to blanket the flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the 
radiometers.  As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity.  The estimates were 
not part of the science requirements and may not have been sufficiently tracked in the hardware 
development.  Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the 
envisioned BRE test duration and 60 times the duration of the drop tests.  With the fixed 
amplification of the radiometer signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge 
that the limits were exceeded.  Saturation of the radiometers was partially mitigated in the round 
2 testing through use of ACME’s standard array instead of the one developed specifically for BRE 
which was used in the first round of testing.

More generally, ACME’s Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) used to control the flow of fuel and 
nitrogen have unfortunately not always performed adequately, where the flow rates have not 
always been appropriately steady.  Steps were made to mitigate such behavior, e.g., by zero-ing 
the MFCs prior to each test, but they were not completely successful.  Furthermore, when an MFC 
is used at a small fraction of its maximum flow rate, the actual flow rate sometimes differs from 
that desired.   
 
During testing on 23 Dec. 2020 (20358), it was discovered that the lowest of the 14-micron silicon 
carbide fibers on the Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array had broken.  After some 
discussion, testing continued that day.  Given that the translating array had five ceramic fibers, 
the loss of one was not a significant science loss.  But it was a concern for crew safety.  Recovery

like array.  Unfortunately, the next fiber was broken during the delicate operations where the 
fibers are only spaced 5 mm apart.  As a result, the last two BRE test days were conducted with 
only three rather than five fibers in the TFP array.  ACME does have alternate fiber arrays, but 
there were months of testing remaining and the decision was made to continue testing with only 
3 fibers.

(19091) that the hot-wire igniter tip had failed on the preceding test day, preventing further flame 
testing until it could be replaced.  While such circumstances are uncommon for ACME operations, 
BRE tests were sometimes conducted under conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and 
deactivation, which led to momentary flashes without sustained ignition.  Given that unplanned 
crew time is required to replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees 
- the igniter voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame.  The latter was known 
from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the hot-wire igniter tip 
and hasten its demise.  It is notable that the flashes of flame (across the burner surface) 
sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was deactivated and retracted.  In one case on the 
first day of testing, there was excess fuel and a ‘fireball’ was ignited which promptly quenched.  
Ignition also sometimes failed due to a software limitation where the fuelFlowIgnitionDeltaMs 
parameter which specifies the relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be evenly 
divisible by 100 (ms).  This limitation wasn’t initially understood and the igniter sometimes didn’t 
energize as a result.

4. Preliminary Results  
The burner has shown that quasi-steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat surface of 25 mm 
diameter.  Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have focused on flame spread with a 
wind for concurrent spread and at least a self-induced wind for opposed flow spread.  We already 
knew that this would be possible from normal-gravity research.  The burning of liquids, as in a wick of 
a candle flame and small droplets, has been shown to produce steady flames.  However, many droplet 
flames were found to extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame.  We see this as well in the 
extended ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for nominal 
ambient conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia.  At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia and 34% 
oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more.  These are all atmospheric 
conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft. 
 
A. Changed Test Plans 
While BRE’s proposal included desired testing with carbon-dioxide-diluted atmospheres, NASA’s 
plan for the ISS investigation did not include desired testing.  Therefore, the exclusion of that 
testing was not a change in plans. 
 
The most significant change was the use of ACME’s standard radiometer array rather than the 
BRE radiometer array in BRE’s second round of testing.  This change was made because the BRE 
array was found to generally saturate during the ISS tests.  The ACME array had a greater range 
but nonetheless still often saturated during testing.   
 
Significant changes were made to the ignition procedure in the early first-round testing, both 
relative to the preceding ACME experiments and in the first few days of BRE testing.  Compared 
to the other ACME burners (neglecting the outer plenum of the coflow burner), the BRE burners 
have a much greater internal volume.  Therefore, the fuel flow was begun before the igniter was 
energized, where that period ranged from a few seconds to roughly 1 minute.  The duration was 
typically about 15 and 30 seconds for the 25- and 50-mm BRE burners, respectively.  In contrast, 
the fuel flow has commonly been started when the igniter is energized in the other ACME 
investigations. 
 
Despite the duration of fuel flow prior to igniter activation, there was concern about 
understanding the composition of the gas initially flowing from the burner.  Therefore, on the 
second BRE test day (20 Feb. 2019, i.e., 19051), a no-flame ‘test’ was run before each flame test 
in which the burner was flushed with nitrogen at 0.15 slpm for 15 seconds.  A shortcoming of this 
measure was that the time between the nitrogen flushing and the start of the fuel flow was not

The CIR experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  Thus far, ACME’s activity

astronauts and cosmonauts exchange gas bottles, mass flow controllers, and igniter tips.  In the

All CIR tests are remotely commanded from the ground from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations 
Center (GIPOC) in Cleveland, Ohio.  Typically, four to six people staff four consoles during the 
testing.  The CIR hardware is controlled from the Rack Officer (RO) and Data Management Officer 
(DMO) consoles, and the ACME hardware is controlled from the Payload Developer (PD) console.  
Two shifts of personnel are scheduled to staff these three consoles on test days because they 
typically last 14 hours with the many pre- and post-testing activities.  Given that the tests are 
remotely commanded, the operations are carried out in the day and evening in Cleveland, e.g., 
from 7 AM to 9 PM.  A day’s tests, i.e., with flames, are normally conducted in a period of 10 hours 
of less.  Tests are normally conducted on three weekdays per two weeks.  On intervening 
weekdays, the image data is downlinked and the crew often swap one or both gas bottles.  
Transferring and downlinking data from a day’s tests also requires a 2-shift day for the RO and 
DMO consoles, where it is always necessary to verify that data was downlinked without errors 
and that data is not missing.  Those two positions are also staffed to guide and oversee the crew 
activity.  As a result, the CIR consoles are normally actively staffed on four weekdays per week.  A 
team of four carry out the detailed planning for the CIR and ACME console staff, and the daily 
operational plans typically exceed 50 pages on days including testing. 
 
The science console allows for review of the analog video and non-imaging telemetry (at 1 Hz) in 
near real time but doesn’t allow for commanding.  In the case of E-FIELD Flames, arrangements 
were made so that the analog video is streamed to a secure computer at UC Irvine to allow the 
research team to participate in test operations and to recommend adjustments to the day’s 
planned parameters.  That team does not see the telemetry during the testing, but is in 
communication via phone and e-mail with their NASA research partners at the GRC ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  While there are many preparatory steps, the tests are ultimately 
conducted using an uploaded software script and parameter files.  In advance of the test day, the 
UC Irvine science team plans the nearly 60 parameters in the voltage sweep script and specifies 
other parameters that are configured outside of the script, such as camera settings.  It is also 
possible to effectively conduct tests in a ‘manual’ mode, where parameters are changed in 
response to the analog video downlink or telemetry.  For example, the electric field potential can 
be adjusted to approach a stability or soot limit. 
 
Provisions have been made to enable the investigators from all ACME experiments to remotely 
view the analog video while they communicated verbally with NASA science personnel in the 
operations center.  Thus far, all ACME flame tests, including those for BRE, have been conducted 
in an automated manner using software scripts and extensive parameter files. 
 
Typically, ten E-FIELD Flames tests are conducted per test day. Despite the short test durations, 
the low rate results from several unavoidable factors.  After a test is conducted, the 125-Hz non-
imaging data is downlinked for immediate review by the science team.  A small sample of images 
are often downlinked to ensure that the camera exposures are appropriate, where the times for 
those images are typically selected based on non-imaging data to provide extreme examples.  The 
review helps to verify parameters or plan for adjustments in subsequent tests, e.g., to select the 
voltage range after determining where the ion current saturates for the given flame conditions.  
After a test is conducted, a fan circulates the chamber atmosphere after which the chamber is 
vented (to space) back to atmospheric pressure, if needed.  Midway through a day’s E-FIELD 
Flames tests, the atmosphere is circulated for 15 minutes through a filter cartridge filled with 
molecular sieves to capture any soot and adsorb at least a portion of the combustion products, 
e.g., carbon dioxide, water vapor, and incomplete combustion products.  The tests are only

constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber.  This resource constraint is 
exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the 
fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow 
in the case of inverse flame testing).  The timers can only be reset by venting the combustion 
chamber.  Therefore, the timer limit combined with other constraints effectively corresponds to 
the day’s maximum flow time for the fuel (or more generally, the limiting reactant).  For E-FIELD 
Flames, the safety timers are set to the maximum value of 999 seconds, which corresponds to the 
10 tests typically completed per day. 
 
The 999-second limit on the valve safety timers has thus far been common for all ACME testing.  
However, the timers can be reset to 999 by nearly completely venting the chamber.  Sufficient time

The experimental flammability maps are shown in Figures 14 and 15.  Both plots indicate a 
decreasing, inverse asymptotic-like curve that approaches zero, for heat of gasification with mass 
flux.  It is surprising that the data cluster about a nearly singular trend.  However, both plots show 
the heat of gasification is up to 20% higher for the lower heat of combustion, 23.6 kJ/g.  Our 
experiments in the University of Maryland lab have shown, with the BRE in 1-g, that similar results 
for propane-nitrogen mixtures have the opposite behavior with heats of gasification decreasing 
with heat of combustion for the same mass flux.  But again, the data mostly cluster about one 
trend line except for very low heats of combustion.  However, the 1-g corresponding heat of 
combustion data shift far to the right and down from the microgravity data of Figures 14 and 15.  
For example, the 1-g data would indicate (𝑚̇”, 𝐿) points of about 30 g/m2s, 2 kJ/g and 10, 0.5.  
Moreover, our previous work in a 5- s drop facility suggested similar data trends but with an 
apparent vertical asymptote at about 3 g/m2s, rather than 1 as shown here.  Obviously, the 
current data at durations of minutes are more accurate than those limited to 5 s.  However, it has 
been shown that the ISS heat flux data even at self-extinction are theoretically nearly steady.  
Figures 14 and 15 include the heats of gasification derived from the self-extinguished endpoint 
data as well.  Remarkably, the self-extinguished not-so-steady data follow the same trend as the 
steady data.  
 
Let us interpret Figures 14 and 15 in terms of the flammability of real materials in microgravity.  
Typical melting plastics have heats of gasification ranging from about 2 to 3 kJ/g, with effective 
heats of gasification for charring plastics above 4 kJ/g.  Some selected literature values for 
materials with heats of combustion in the BRE range are listed in Table 2.  The accuracy of the 
calorimeter heat flux is found to be less than the two sensors, thus, we relied on the arithmetic 
average of the two heat flux sensors data for obtaining the flammability map.  However, same 
results are shown considering the calorimeter data.  Figure 14 would suggest that polyethylene 
(PE) and polypropylene (PP) would burn in microgravity at about 3 g/m2s.  Nylon and PMMA would 
burn at about 2.5 g/m2s, and the phenolic glass fiber composite would burn at about 1 g/m2s.  
 
 
 
BRE tests in orbit were finished with 196 successful ignitions. The measured heat flux and the end 
point data of the long duration tests (i.e., the tests that fuel was terminated as opposed to the 
tests that self-extinguished) were used to obtain heats of gasification.  The measured heat flux for 
all quasi steady tests are shown in Fig. 14.  The heats of gasification of these data from all the tests 
vs. fuel mixture mass flux are shown in Fig. 15.  One important fire safety consideration, based on 
the findings of this study, is that solid materials with heats of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 
kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity.  The NASA 
alternative flammability Test 2 [1] using the Cone Calorimeter can measure these material 
properties. As this study develops a more complete understanding, NASA may wish to put more 
emphasis into Test 2.

D. Surprises and New Discoveries  
Initial surprises and discoveries include: 
(1) It is found out that quasi-steady burning on a flat surface, representing a pool fire, can 
exist in microgravity. Ambient oxygen mole fraction plays the most significant role in this 
regard. The quasi-steady flames were observed for nominal ambient oxygen mole 
fractions of 0.265 and above.  
(2) Although ambient pressure has a weak effect on the quality of burning, it affects radiative 
heat loss by changing the partial pressures of radiating species, i.e., H2O and CO2.  
(3) Methane nitrogen-generated flames self-extinguished within a minute for all ambient 
conditions.  That indicates that the burn time depends on the fuel chemistry. 
(4) Ethylene flames, which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions, did not soot under 
microgravity conditions. Sooting only occurred upon ignition and disappeared quickly 
after ignition.  Nitrogen dilution reduced the amount of soot. 
(5) Radiative loss fraction for the flames in microgravity can reach about 60% compared to 
30% for the normal gravity flames. 
(6) TFP measurements of four flames confirmed that critical temperature range for extinction 
is 1100 to 1200 K.  This is confirmed by numerical simulations.  
(7) A It was shown that the BRE can emulate several liquids and solids including Acetone, 
Ethanol, Methanol, PMMA, Nylon, Phenolic glass fiber, etc. as demonstrated by a 
flammability diagram, as a plot of heats of gasification vs. the mass burning rate, based 
on the steady average surface heat flux. 
(8) For the first time, two limits of extinction were obtained on a plot of heat of combustion 
vs. heats of gasification.  The plot shows the flammability region for each nominal ambient 
oxygen mole fraction with radiative extinction for large flames and another extinction 
limit for small flames.

The objectives are presented here with brief summaries of the findings; readers are 
encouraged to refer to section 4.C for more information. 
 
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25- and 50-mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients 
with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-considered 
atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2 psia, 
26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a 
diverse range of condensed fuels.  
An elevated oxygen concentration in the ambient enhanced flammability and quasi-
steady flames for nominal oxygen mole fractions of 0.265 and above. Pressure had a 
minimal effect on the quality of burning.  The microgravity flames corresponded to the 
combustion of a range of liquid and solid fuels. 
 
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambient of O2/CO2 (desired).  
As planned, this objective was not investigated in the conducted tests.  It would be a good 
candidate for further exploration in a follow-on experiment. 
 
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.  
All flames ignited in normal atmosphere self-extinguished within 40 s.  In contrast, oxygen 
mole fractions of 0.265 and above resulted in quasi-steady flames.  Large flames 
extinguished due to radiative heat loss, while small flames quenched at a second limit.  
 
F. Additional Objectives Achieved 
An empirical correlation for the radiative loss fraction was obtained through a dimensional 
analysis of the radiation data.  The correlation was used to predict the flames’ radiative loss 
fractions from their mass burning rate, oxygen mole fraction in the ambient, chamber pressure, 
and heat of combustion.  This result was used to correct the heat of combustion in the analytical 
solution for these flames. 
 
G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products 
BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety.  Quasi-steady burning 
corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in 
microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established 
step in putting out spacecraft fires.  The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen 
in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas 
such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time. 
 
 
While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its 
alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material 
properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.  
 
H. Patents 
Thus far, no patents have been filed from the BRE research.

I.  Introduction 
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity 
Experiments (ACME) project.  BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.  More specifically, 
BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as 
extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the 
relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.  A flat 
porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where 
measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the 
vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.  A small number of gaseous fuels (including 
mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and 
alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and gasification, the surface 
temperature, and smoke point.   The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 
 
1 Feb. 2022 
46 
 
directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an 
efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammability and selecting fire-
resistant spacecraft materials. 
BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA 
does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B. 
A. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients 
with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-considered 
atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2 
psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to 
a diverse range of condensed fuels. 
B. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 
C. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.  
The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e., 
liquids and non-charring plastics). 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  With these advantages, microgravity 
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  
The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The most 
common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and 
the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. 
 
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload 
Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a 
nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in

stream.  For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady data has been 
collected.  But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far for BRE or 
ACME in general. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. 
 
 
III.  Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, where a total of 45 flames were 
ignited during Increment 58.  That round was completed in April 2019, where the latter 
portion will be covered in the upcoming Increment 59-60 report.  Meanwhile, the second 
round of BRE testing is expected to begin near the end of Increment 60 and continue into 
Increment 61.  The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in 
advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that 
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
All of the first round of tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while 
burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen.  The tests were carried out 
at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of 
possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats.  More specifically, testing 
was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; (2) 10.2 
psia, 26.5 %; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.  In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with 
nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) 
from preceding tests. 
 
BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both 
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) 
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the 
absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because 
of its carbon double bond.  Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with 
nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch for 
some cases.  But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and 
nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of 
fuel concentrations.

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
1. Mission anomalies  
There were no significant anomalies hindering BRE operations during Increment 58. 
 
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often 
saturated.  Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment 
success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own 
radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.  Estimates had been made of 
the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the 
flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the 
radiometers.  As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity.  The 
estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been 
sufficiently tracked in the hardware development.  Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted 
as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60

times the duration of the drop tests.  With the fixed amplification of the radiometer 
signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were 
exceeded.  An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE 
testing continued unchanged. 
 
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere: 
The radiometry array proved problematic as its sensors were mostly out of range 
and quickly became saturated.  However, for some of the small size flames, these 
data were complete.  Those data will be vital to assessing the role of flame and 
combustion product radiation in the destiny of the flames. 
 
Ignition was not always successful, where BRE tests were sometimes conducted under 
conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to momentary 
flashes without sustained ignition.  Given that unplanned crew time is required to 
replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees - the igniter 
voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame.  The latter was known 
from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the hot-wire 
igniter tip and hasten its demise.  It is notable that the flashes of flame (across the 
burner surface) sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was deactivated and 
retracted.  In one case on the first day of testing, there was excess fuel and a ‘fireball’ 
was ignited which promptly quenched.  Ignition also sometimes failed due to a 
software limitation where the fuelFlowIgnitionDeltaMs parameter which specifies the 
relative timing of the fuel flow and igniter activation must be evenly divisible by 100 
(ms).  This limitation wasn’t initially understood and the igniter didn’t energize as a 
result. 
 
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere: 
It was realized that the igniter for the burner gases could only be applied for up to 
4 seconds, on insertion and retraction.  This produced an unanticipated problem, 
as the time for the burner gases to reach the igniter could be 10s of seconds 
depending on the set flow rate.  Also, after the first test, the burner would contain 
that fuel mixture minus diffusion with the chamber.  Thus the burner would need 
to be flushed with nitrogen before the second fuel mixture was initiated.    
 
Intense communication with the NASA team proceeded the day before the first 
test. The gas volume of the burner along with the feed pipe volume was supplied 
by NASA.  Accordingly ground experiments at Maryland were conducted with an 
identical NASA BRE burner along with its piping volume from the flow valve.   
These experiments and theory were used to develop an algorithm for determining 
the relative timing of the igniter and gas flow activation that will result in ignition. 
 
Day 1 was conducted with rough estimates made on the fly, and fortunately nearly 
all of the tests led to a satisfactory ignition.  By Day 2 an algorithm was established

D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere) 
All of Round 1 tests have had the thermopile sensor data reduced using their original 
calibrations.  As presented immediately below, the data must be continually processed to 
address the effect of the combustion product water and any paint degradation. 
 
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from 
the flame to the burner surface.  In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass 
flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated 
fuel.  The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of 
gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in 
an inert matrix).  Thus achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real 
solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity.  Other than a candle flame, this has 
not been shown before.

The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface.  
One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center.  The resulting data suffered 
from two possible effects.   The first effect is the condensation of water vapor.  As the 
sensors are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its 
combustion products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor.  This occurs, as 
the dew point for combustion products is about 60 – 70 oC, and the sensor begins at 
ambient temperature and can achieve temperatures over 100 oC.  Thus condensation can 
occur at temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor.  Above 
the dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor.  
Once the sensor is dry, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases as intended.  
 
We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1-g laboratory experiments with our 
duplicative NASA BRE burner.  The figure below (Fig. 1) shows an illustration of the 
condensation and evaporation effect in the ISS tests.   The offset sensor in red shows a 
clear jump increase when the water fully evaporates.    More analysis is needed to 
properly correct for this effect.  Fortunately by the end of the test shown here (and for all 
of the other data), this water effect is gone.

E. Preliminary Research Findings (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere) 
Despite having much data to digest and completely analyze, there is a profound 
conclusion from these tests.  The burner has definitively shown that steady burning is 
possible for real solids with a flat surface of 25 mm diameter.  Up to now most 
flammability studies in microgravity have focused on flame spread with a wind for 
concurrent spread and at least a self-induced wind for opposed flow spread.  We already 
knew that this would be possible from 1-g research.   The burning of liquids, as in a wick 
of a candle flame and small droplets, has been shown to produce steady flames.  
However, in the case of droplet burning cool flames could sustain normal burning, and 
normal burning would extinguish.  The extinction has been shown to result from the 
radiative cooling of the flame.  We see this as well in the extended ISS microgravity tests.  
However this extinction was predominately seen for atmospheric conditions of 21 %

solids.  This will be significant when the totality of results for the 25 mm flat burning

single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the ISS’ 
Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  The investigation will be carried out in two separate rounds, 
where the first round began in Increment 58 and was completed in Increment 59, so there is 
nothing to be reported for Increment 60.  The second round of testing will be conducted in 
Increments 61 and/or 62.

I.  Introduction 
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack 
(CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity 
Experiments (ACME) project.  BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.  More specifically, 
BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as 
extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the 
relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.  A flat 
porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where 
measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the 
vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.  A small number of gaseous fuels (including 
mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and

temperature, and smoke point.   The experiment’s results can establish fuel properties that 
directly relate to fire hazards in spacecraft, and if effective in microgravity could provide an 
efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for assessing flammability and selecting fire-
resistant spacecraft materials. 
 
BRE’s specific experimental objectives are as follows, where it must be emphasized that NASA 
does not currently plan to carry out the desired tests for objective B. 
D. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 
mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients 
with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA-considered 
atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; 10.2 
psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to 
a diverse range of condensed fuels. 
E. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 
F. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.  
The observations will enable quantification of the microgravity behavior of condensed fuels (i.e., 
liquids and non-charring plastics). 
 
Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages 
over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., 
gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length 
scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  
Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be 
studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger 
sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-
gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in 
microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot 
free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and 
stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  With these advantages, microgravity 
testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the 
gravitational environment of the combustion application. 
 
 
II.  Methods/Research Operations 
  
A. Discussion of Method/Protocol 
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  
The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The most 
common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and 
the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.

All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the 
NASA Glenn Research Center.  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in 
a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately 
be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in 
response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry 
stream.  For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady data has been 
collected.  But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far for BRE or 
ACME in general. 
 
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to 
ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. 
 
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary 
analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing. 
 
 
III. Results 
A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight 
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, where a total of 45 flames were 
ignited during Increment 58.  That round was completed in April 2019, during the 
beginning of Increment 59, when an additional 17 flames were ignited.  As such, a total 
of 62 flames were ignited in the first round of testing.  Meanwhile, the second round of 
BRE testing is expected to begin near the end of Increment 61 and continue into 
Increment 62.  The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in 
advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that 
knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome. 
 
All of the first round of tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while 
burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen.  The tests were carried out 
at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of 
possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats.  More specifically, testing 
was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 
10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen.  In all cases, the atmosphere was 
diluted with nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and 
carbon dioxide) from preceding tests.  An exception is tests conducted after the chamber 
atmosphere was vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day.  But the atmosphere 
was typically refreshed once during each of testing.  
 
BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are 
independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both 
are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) 
is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the 
absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting

B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies 
1. Mission anomalies  
There were no significant anomalies hindering BRE operations during Increment 59, 
but there was one in Increment 58 during the preparations for BRE testing began (that 
was mistakenly not addressed in the 30-day report including that increment).  It was 
discovered on Feb. 4 (GMT 035) that the pressure was low in a check gas bottle for 
the CIR’s Gas Chromatograph Instrumentation Package (GCIP).  The bottle had been 
on the space station for 9 years, and the low pressure was attributed to a nominal 
leak rate.  The check gas was for calibration of the GCIP measurements and not 
needed for regular operations which proceeded unhindered.  The bottle was replaced 
on June 13 to enable the necessary calibration. 
 
2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data   
BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often 
saturated.  Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment 
success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own 
radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.  Estimates had been made of 
the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the 
flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the 
radiometers.  As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity.  The 
estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been 
sufficiently tracked in the hardware development.  Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted 
as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60 
times the duration of the drop tests.  With the fixed amplification of the radiometer 
signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were 
exceeded.  An engineering review failed to identify an acceptable solution and BRE 
testing continued unchanged. 
 
From the BRE PI Jim Quintiere: 
The radiometry array proved problematic as its sensors were mostly out of range 
and quickly became saturated.  However, for some of the small size flames, these 
data were complete.  Those data will be vital to assessing the role of flame and 
combustion product radiation. 
 
Ignition was not always successful.  As previously discussed, it was discovered on 
April 1 (GMT 091) that the hot-wire igniter tip had failed on the preceding test day, 
preventing further flame testing until it could be replaced.  While such circumstances 
are uncommon for ACME operations, BRE tests were sometimes conducted under 
conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to momentary 
flashes without sustained ignition.  Given that unplanned crew time is required to 
replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees - the igniter 
voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame.  The latter was known 
from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the hot-wire

C. Completeness/Quality of Data 
The number of flames ignited in Increments 58 and 59 significantly exceeds the planned 
tests – under the tested conditions (25 mm burner and ethylene as fuel) - which were 
specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD).  A 
total of 25 such tests were required, while 62 flames with those conditions were ignited.  
As such, more than twice as many flames were ignited as had been planned.  
 
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not necessarily available for 
all tests.  Recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is done 
because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed 
per test day.  Given the constraint, the decision is sometimes made to sacrifice some 
image data (e.g., from the HiBMs camera) to allow additional tests to be conducted.  This 
is intentionally done to maximize the scientific return of each day of testing within the 
project constraints. 
 
From BRE Co-I Peter Sunderland: 
The video and image data of the testing produced satisfactory data to display the 
nature of the burning sequence from ignition to self-extinction or fuel termination. 
However, the image quality is less than was hoped for. The ACME ops camera provides 
video, but only offers 0.3 megapixels of resolution, and for many flames it is too 
zoomed out. The GigE camera has poor sensitivity in the blue, and after the ignition 
transient all our flames have been blue. This camera only offers 1.4 megapixels of 
resolution and requires about 1 s exposures for blue flames, which is far too slow to 
be considered video. The images provided by both cameras are, according to UMD 
marketing staff, at too low resolution to be used in press releases. In round 2 we will 
increase the gain on the GigE camera, an option we were unaware of in round 1. 
 
Data quality is of course dependent on the experimental hardware.  But neglecting that 
limitation on data quality, the cameras are sensitive to radiation where pixels gradually 
become ‘hot’ over time.  While these bright spots are addressed in image post-processing, 
they are a degradation of the image quality.

D. Status of Data Analysis (submitted by BRE PI Jim Quintiere and doctoral student 
Parham Dehghani) 
All measured transient raw data (e.g., heat flux sensors, thermocouples, radiometers, 
mass flow meters and chamber pressure sensor) have been converted to engineering 
units and plotted using the calibrations provided in ACME’s Software Interface Design 
Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D).  
 
All of the round 1 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their original 
calibrations.  As presented below, the data is being processed to address the effect of the 
combustion product water and paint degradation. 
 
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from 
the flame to the burner surface.  In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass 
flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated 
fuel.  The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of 
gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in 
an inert matrix).  Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real 
solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity.  Other than for a candle flame, this 
has not been shown before. 
 
The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface.  
One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center.  The resulting data suffered 
from two possible effects.   The first effect is the condensation of water vapor.  As the 
sensors are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its 
combustion products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor.  This occurs, as 
the dew point for combustion products is about 60-70oC, and the sensor begins at 
ambient temperature and can achieve temperatures over 100oC.  Thus, condensation can 
occur at temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor.  Above 
the dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor.
